description: We are a passionate crew of 6, blending core Software Engineering and AI expertise with strong interpersonal skills and a relentless drive to learn. We thrive on innovation, bold ideas, and building tech that matters. We're currently looking for creative minds to join our mission, share the journey, and push boundaries together. Let’s build the future!
summary:
What did we build? StellarOp Mission Lab is a game that runs in any web browser. One to four players design,
launch and fly one complete space mission together. Each player takes a role: Science Lead, Communications
Lead, Spacecraft Engineer or Mission Planner. Each role watches a short briefing from a guide, then the team
chooses instruments, antenna, ground stations, power, battery, orbit and launch vehicle.
What problem does it solve? Students rarely get to try a whole mission, from the first idea to operations. Real
missions are a set of trade-offs: more instruments need more power, more data needs a bigger antenna, a
heavier satellite needs a bigger rocket. Mission Lab lets beginners feel these trade-offs by playing them.
How does it answer the challenge? The challenge asks for a game where a team designs, manages and
simulates a space mission. In Mission Lab every choice costs mass, power, data, budget or lifetime. The
mission then flies in 3D, random events test the design, and a final report explains why the mission succeeded
or failed and compares it with the real NASA mission it is based on.
Who could it help, and why does it matter? Students, teachers and anyone curious about how missions are
planned. It teaches mission design by doing, in plain English and Egyptian Arabic, and a wrong choice is
explained instead of only marked wrong
details:
What it does StellarOp Mission Lab takes a team through one complete space mission, from the first idea to the final report. The team reads real mission facts in short briefings, makes design choices that each cost mass, power, data, budget or lifetime, launches, flies the mission in 3D, handles surprises, and learns why the mission worked or failed. Main task. Input: the team's choices (instruments, antenna, ground stations, power, battery, orbit, launch vehicle) and their votes on events. Process: the game adds up mass, power, data, budget and lifetime, checks them against the mission needs and the rocket capacity, then simulates the flight. Output: a live 3D flight, a score out of 1000, stars, a decision table with reasons, and a comparison with the real NASA mission. How the game is played, screen by screen The screenshots below come from the live game at https://mohamdkhaldd.github.io/stellarop-mission-lab/. They follow one player through Level 1 (Khamsin Storm Watch), from the first page to the certificate

Opening the game The game starts on the home screen. The team chooses how to play: Play Solo, Team on One Computer, Online Team (each player on their own laptop) or Mission Architect (6 more missions and a Sandbox). The strip at the bottom shows the four moves of every level: watch your guide, write on the team board, decide together, launch and see who you helped
Signing in (optional) The Sign in button in the top bar opens the player account window, where a player can use Google or an email and password. Nothing is blocked without it; signing in only saves finished levels so they follow the player to any device
Choosing a level Next, the team picks a level. The four levels follow NASA JPL's Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1 to 4); each is a different real mission and each is harder than the one before. Level 1 is open. The others unlock when the team earns at least one star, but judges and teachers can press Unlock all levels to open every level at once
The briefings Inside a level, the team starts with the briefings. Each role has a guide, and the Mission Director gives the first one (briefing 1 of 5 in the picture). The guide's video lasts about a minute and gives the real numbers for that role. The script is shown under the video, with the numbers highlighted. When a video ends, the player writes the numbers on the shared team board, because later screens show names only. The Next briefing button moves on to the next guide. When all briefings are done, the team talks together about what everyone learned, and then moves on to the design. Watching a video again costs 20 points
Designing the satellite After the discussion, the team makes its design choices. Each role has its own questions (Science Lead, Communications Lead, Spacecraft Engineer, Mission Planner). In the picture the Communications Lead chooses between a slow and a fast antenna, and the answer depends on the numbers written on the team board. The 3D satellite changes with every part the team adds. The team starts with 1,000 points and loses points for needs not met, wasted parts, damage in flight, space junk, extra design reviews and rewatching videos. The first design review is free and shows hidden problems. When every role has chosen, the team presses Launch
Launch The launch starts with real NASA/SpaceX footage (the PACE launch on Falcon 9, 2024), then the game switches to the 3D flight. A satellite that is too heavy for its rocket falls. The bars at the bottom show the spacecraft's health and the team's points
Surprises in flight During the flight, 2 to 3 random events appear. This one is Eclipse season: for about an hour each night, Earth's shadow covers the satellite. The team talks, then votes. The best answer depends on the parts they chose; here the satellite has solar panels and a battery, so the team decides how to get through the shadow
Who used the data When the flight ends, the game shows the user segment: who used the mission's data. For Level 1 these are Egypt's weather forecasters, airports and people with asthma. This teaches the four segments NASA uses for every mission: launch, space, ground and users
The mission report Then the report appears. It shows the stars (400, 700 and 900 points) and whether the needs were met. A table lists every decision, the points it cost and why. The report also lists what the team did well and what to fix next time, and it compares the design with the real NASA mission, with a 3D model of that mission. The team can redesign and fly again
The certificate At the end, the team writes its names and downloads a certificate of mission success for that level. Then the team goes back to the level screen and plays the next level
